title: Planar Interfaces for Transmission of Chiral Spin Textures
authors: Robin Msiska, Cynthia J. O. Reichhardt, Charles Reichhardt, Eric Fullerton, Avadh Saxena
abstract: Lateral magnetic interfaces provide a direct way to test whether skyrmions remain robust when driven across abrupt changes in material parameters and magnetic order. Here we study skyrmion transmission across planar ferromagnet-ferromagnet (FM-FM), antiferromagnet-antiferromagnet (AFM-AFM), ferromagnet-antiferromagnet (FM-AFM), and antiferromagnet-ferromagnet (AFM-FM) interfaces using micromagnetic simulations and analytic reduced-coordinate criteria. The outcomes are organized into phase diagrams according to the morphology formed in the receiving region, distinguishing compact transmission from deformed skyrmions, stripe-domain states, amorphous textures, and relaxation into the background. Same-order FM-FM and AFM-AFM skyrmion transmission is captured by an analytically defined range of the reduced Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction, identifying the wall-softening regime that supports compact transmission without stripe formation. Mixed-order FM-AFM and AFM-FM interfaces are directionally distinct, requiring conversion between ferromagnetic magnetization and antiferromagnetic Néel textures. These results show that planar interfaces act as active transport elements and provide reduced design criteria for heterogeneous skyrmion tracks.
summary: This paper analyzes the transmission of magnetic skyrmions across various planar interfaces (e.g., FM/AFM). Using micromagnetic simulations, the authors demonstrate that these interfaces function as active transport elements whose behavior is dictated by the specific magnetic order change. The results provide reduced design criteria for engineering functional spintronic devices.
main_problem: The study investigates how chiral spin textures, specifically skyrmions, maintain their structural integrity when driven across abrupt material interfaces with varying magnetic order.
main_result: Planar interfaces act as active transport elements, and the transmission outcome (e.g., compact vs. deformed) depends critically on the interface type (FM-FM, FM-AFM, etc.) and underlying material parameters.
method: The research employs continuum micromagnetic simulations combined with analytic reduced-coordinate criteria to map out phase diagrams for skyrmion transmission.
model_or_system: The system is an ultrathin film modeled by the Landau–Lifshitz–Gilbert equation, considering four types of planar interfaces (FM-FM, AFM-AFM, FM-AFM, AFM-FM). The energy functional includes bulk terms and explicit interface coupling energies.
key_observables: Skyrmion transmission outcome classified as compact transmission, deformed skyrmions, stripe-domain states, amorphous textures, or relaxation into the background.
important_parameters: Reduced Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interaction (DMI), effective anisotropy, and dimensionless chirality ratios ($\kappa$).
main_assumptions: The material parameters are assumed to be piecewise constant across the interface; the model uses micromagnetic approximations for texture dynamics.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates the general source-receiving geometry and provides block representations for the four studied planar interface classes.
paper_structure: The paper systematically develops the governing equations (LLG, energy functional) for different interface types, derives specific boundary conditions at the interface ($\Gamma$), analyzes the resulting phase diagrams using reduced parameters, and concludes by classifying interfaces as active transport elements.
why_interesting: While focused on magnetism, the concept of 'active transport' across engineered boundaries, governed by local field equations and energy minimization principles, shares conceptual links with open quantum systems dynamics where boundary conditions dictate system evolution.
